04 · Read & review

The transcript

Submit all six answers to unlock the transcript. You can then listen and read together.

Emma regarded the redacted copy of Helen Ward's family letter as a modest but important advance: for the first time, she could examine a document linked by a potential witness to an actual application, rather than another uncompleted template. Its evidential value, however, depended on restrictions she had agreed to respect and checks she had yet to perform.

Helen's cousin had authorised confidential examination of a scanned copy, not publication. Personal identifiers and course details had been obscured. Emma confirmed those terms in writing, limited access within the newsroom and avoided treating the possession of a scan as a licence to disclose its contents indiscriminately.

Comparison with Fiona Bell's unused decision-notice template produced encouraging similarities in layout and wording, particularly the paragraph about the fourteen-day review procedure. Such consistency was relevant to provenance, but hardly dispositive. The template might have been widely available; the scan might omit later pages; neither possibility had been tested.

A final sentence proved more instructive than the matching typography: “Payment subject to final verification.” Selection was stated; a transfer was not. There was no remittance confirmation, banking reference or evidence that the student had satisfied the outstanding conditions.

Sarah asked whether Helen could find a bank statement or subsequent correspondence. Emma sent a restrained enquiry. Helen replied that she would consult her cousin, without promising more information or access. The relative's decision would govern any additional disclosure.

Fiona's parallel investigation of the trust's archive yielded a new category of material: a list of payment authorisations. Fiona cautioned that the list had not been reconciled with banking records or examined in full. An authorisation could permit expenditure without establishing that funds had left an account, much less reached the intended beneficiary. Privacy constraints also ruled out releasing identifiable applicants' details.

The development returned Emma to a line she had recorded weeks earlier. An unidentified caller had urged her to ask who signed off payments rather than concentrate solely on missing minutes. The caller's motives and knowledge remained unknown. Yet the newly located records gave that instruction a possible documentary route. Emma refused to elevate the anonymous warning into corroboration of itself.

She revised her working categories: Selected, Authorised, Transferred. A difference among those populations would not, by itself, demonstrate fraud. Applications could be withdrawn, conditions remain unmet, transfers be reversed or entries fall in different reporting periods. The task was to establish both what had occurred and which explanation best accounted for it.

Sarah asked whether the selected student described in Helen's letter could be traced through the authorisation list. Emma ruled out using restricted foundation records to identify the cousin. A voluntarily shared, appropriately redacted payment record might permit a narrower comparison, but no such permission or record yet existed.

Near the end of the day Fiona sent one more inventory detail: a heading reading “Payment exceptions — 2011”. She had not inspected the contents and could not say what an exception represented. Sarah's immediate suspicion was understandable, but an administrative exception might be an ordinary delay, correction or reversal rather than an irregular transfer.

Emma wrote the heading beside the caller's words, leaving a space between them. Their apparent connection was a hypothesis, not a finding. The next question was no longer simply who had been selected. It was what the trust meant by an exception—and whether any independently verified bank transaction lay behind it.
